summary: A softer US tone on Iran as oil falls, a coalition race in Israel, a senior Russian team for Abu Dhabi talks, missiles over Riyadh, and COP31 opens.

question.text: Dozens of US towns just voted to limit AI data centres over power and water. If many more places do the same, what might happen two or three steps later, for where AI is built, what it costs, and who pays for electricity?

read.title: Interactive: Who wants what at the COP31 climate change summit
read.summary: A clear map of the main fights at COP31, from finance and adaptation to fossil fuels, and where about 100 countries and blocs stand on each.

topics.heading: Tankers burn near Hormuz as Trump calls new strikes on Iran "highly unlikely"
topics.summary: Several ships caught fire in and near the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, and Iran's Revolutionary Guards and a shipping monitor give different accounts.[^2][^4] Trump says new US strikes are "highly unlikely" if talks progress and meets Qatar's prime minister on Monday; oil fell again.[^5][^3][^8]

lead.title: Iran war live: Trump to talk to Xi, Putin about Tehran, 'denuclearisation'

alsoReported.title: Iran live updates: Americans are tired of 'Forever Wars,' Araghchi says
Oil falls as Trump signals restraint on Iran amid fresh Hormuz attacks

article: Over the weekend, several ships caught fire in and near the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carried about a fifth of the world's oil and gas shipments before the war began on Feb 28.[^8] Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) first said two tankers hit mines on an "unauthorised route", then said three were on fire.[^2] The UK's maritime monitor, UKMTO, reported one tanker hit by an "unknown projectile" and a separate fire off Khasab in Oman, with crews safe, and the UAE rescued 22 sailors from a burning cargo ship.[^2][^4]

The US is tightening pressure. The White House says Task Force Iron Gate, which aims to choke Iran's land and sea supply routes, is in "full force and effect"; the IRGC calls it "a play on words".[^2][^3] A drone of unknown origin hit the Khor Mor gas field in Iraqi Kurdistan, and the regional government says it lost about 2.8 gigawatts of power generation.[^3]

Yet Washington's tone has softened. President Trump told CNN that a return to war is "highly unlikely" if talks on Iran's nuclear programme and on reopening Hormuz make progress, and he meets Qatar's prime minister, the main mediator, at the White House on Monday.[^8][^3] He says he will discuss Iran with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin at next week's APEC summit in China.[^5][^3] Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, says Iran's proposal stands but the US must first meet its conditions, including an end to the war "on all fronts".[^4]

G7 foreign ministers meeting in Paris on Nov 9-10 want shipping back to normal and no new US strikes.[^6] Markets are betting on calm: Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell about 16% last week, its steepest weekly drop since early in the pandemic, and slipped below $97 a barrel on Monday.[^7][^8] An analyst told The National prices could fall further if calm holds but warned new attacks could reverse that.[^8] My read: talk and pressure now run side by side, and the test this week is whether Qatar's visit turns softer words into a date for direct talks.
topics.differences: The IRGC blames mines on routes it had warned ships away from; UKMTO describes a projectile strike, and no outside source has confirmed what caused each fire.[^2][^4] Trump says Iran wants a deal "very badly"; Araghchi says the US must meet Iran's requirements first.[^6][^4]

topics.heading: Eisenkot formally gets the mandate to form Israel's government; Knesset sits Tuesday
topics.summary: President Herzog formally handed Gadi Eisenkot the mandate on Sunday, giving him 28 days, plus up to 14 more, to build a 61-seat majority.[^9][^10] He meets Avigdor Liberman on Monday, and the new Knesset is sworn in on Tuesday.[^11] In Lod, police arrested 11 people after a far-right march through an Arab neighbourhood ended in a brawl.[^12]

lead.title: 'Unconventional steps required': Eisenkot vows to form emergency gov't as Herzog bestows mandate

alsoReported.title: President Herzog taps Eisenkot to form coalition, but path remains fraught
11 arrested in Lod brawl after far-right 'sovereignty march' in Arab neighborhood

article: At the President's Residence in Jerusalem on Sunday, Isaac Herzog formally asked Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief who leads the Yashar party, to form Israel's next government.[^9] Herzog said Eisenkot has the "clear and unequivocal support" of a majority: 67 of 120 lawmakers recommended him, including the two Arab-led parties, against 46 for Benjamin Netanyahu.[^9] Eisenkot said "creative and unconventional" steps would be needed and called for a "national emergency government".[^9]

Recommending someone is not the same as joining his government. Eisenkot's own bloc has 48 seats and Netanyahu's 53.[^9] One route to 61 adds the two ultra-Orthodox parties, but Shas calls reports it could join "total fake news".[^10] Another relies on Arab parties backing him from outside: Haaretz reports that Ra'am would, but Avigdor Liberman, whose party is in Eisenkot's bloc, rules out any government that depends on them.[^13][^11] The two men meet on Monday.[^11] Eisenkot has also invited Likud members, though not Netanyahu, to join.[^10]

Netanyahu instead calls for a "national unity government" with his far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies, warning that Israel "simply won't survive" otherwise; Eisenkot's party called his message "hysterical".[^10] National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir has called the Oct 27 election "stolen" without offering evidence.[^13]

Tensions showed on the street. Late Sunday, far-right activists led a "sovereignty march" through an Arab neighbourhood of Lod, a mixed Arab-Jewish city near Tel Aviv. Police arrested 11 people after a brawl; the mayor said there were injuries and arrests on both sides, and police denied reports of a stabbing.[^12] In Gaza, local medical sources say Israeli strikes killed two people on Sunday, and Gaza's health ministry counts 1,610 deaths since the truce began in October 2025.[^14] My read: a new government will take weeks, and how it is built will shape both Gaza policy and Arab-Jewish relations inside Israel.
topics.differences: Eisenkot's camp says a clear majority asked for change; Netanyahu says a government relying on Arab parties would endanger Israel.[^9][^10] Inside Eisenkot's bloc, Liberman and other hawks oppose relying on Arab parties, while Haaretz reports Ra'am is ready to back him.[^11][^13]

topics.heading: Russia sends a senior team to Abu Dhabi talks as strikes cut power to 850,000
topics.summary: Russia has upgraded its team for US-mediated talks with Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on Nov 10-11, the first three-way talks since February.[^17] Over the weekend, Russian strikes left about 850,000 Ukrainians without power, and Ukraine says Moscow is raising pressure before the talks.[^15][^16]

lead.title: Russia Sends High-Level Delegation to Abu Dhabi Talks

alsoReported.title: Russian strikes on Ukraine leave hundreds of thousands without electricity
Russian strikes on Ukraine leave 850,000 without power as Zelenskyy reports drone attack on Komyshuvakha

article: On Tuesday and Wednesday, negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US meet in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates.[^17] Russia's team is led by presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky and now includes two deputy foreign ministers and the head of military intelligence; Bloomberg and Reuters, as cited by the Kyiv Post, say the upgrade may signal more serious engagement.[^17] Ukraine's team is led by former defence minister Rustem Umerov.[^29]

The fighting has not paused. Russian strikes on the power grid on Saturday left more than 600,000 people without electricity in the Dnipropetrovsk region and about 250,000 in the Kharkiv region, where power was later restored, according to the energy company DTEK and officials.[^15][^16] Russia's defence ministry says it will keep striking energy sites it calls linked to the military.[^15] President Zelensky says Russia used about 115 missiles, 1,900 guided bombs and over 3,000 drones in a week, and accuses Moscow of escalating to pressure Kyiv before the talks.[^16]

The gaps are wide. Russia rejects an unconditional ceasefire and demands that Ukraine give up all of the Donbas region, including land Ukraine still holds.[^29] On the US side, Jared Kushner has proposed a five-part framework for European security, which Kyiv and European capitals say lacks ways to enforce it.[^17] President Trump says both sides "for the first time want to make a deal".[^17] France's foreign minister says Europeans will be represented in Abu Dhabi, and European ministers at the G7 in Paris plan to press the US not to push Ukraine into bad terms.[^6]

What to watch: whether the talks produce something limited but real, such as a pause in energy strikes or a prisoner exchange. My read: a full settlement is unlikely this week, because the two sides still disagree on territory and on who would guarantee any deal.
topics.differences: Russia says its strikes hit energy sites tied to Ukraine's military; Ukraine says they aim to black out civilians before winter.[^15][^16] Trump says both sides now want a deal; Kyiv and European capitals say the US security framework lacks enforcement.[^17]

topics.heading: Houthi missiles aimed at Riyadh damage an Aramco tower as Saudi strikes hit Yemen
topics.summary: Saudi Arabia says it intercepted missiles fired by Yemen's Houthi movement at Riyadh and the oil-rich east, and falling debris damaged an Aramco office building without injuring anyone.[^18][^19] The Houthi-run health ministry says Saudi strikes near Sanaa killed at least 33 people.[^18]

lead.title: Aramco building in Riyadh damaged in attempted attack, ministry says

alsoReported.title: Saudi Aramco tower damaged after Houthi missile attacks on Riyadh

article: On Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said it shot down two ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh, then two cruise missiles, plus another ballistic missile aimed at the Eastern Province, home to much of the kingdom's oil industry.[^18][^19] Saudi Arabia's energy ministry says falling fragments caused minor damage to an office building of Aramco, the state oil company, and no one was hurt. A Reuters witness saw windows blown out on several floors of the Aramco tower in Riyadh's financial district.[^18][^19]

The Houthis, an armed movement that controls Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and much of the north, claim six attacks on Riyadh's main airport and several oil sites; these claims have not been independently verified.[^18][^19] Their spokesman says attacks will continue until what he calls the "aggression" and blockade end.[^18] The Houthi-run health ministry says Saudi air strikes on Saturday killed at least 33 people near Sanaa and wounded 39; Saudi authorities say they are investigating.[^18]

Some background: Saudi Arabia and the Houthis largely stopped fighting under a UN-brokered truce in 2022. That calm collapsed when fighting resumed in July, and Yemen's internationally recognised government launched an offensive on Sanaa last month.[^18][^19] The Houthis are long-time allies of Iran, so this front is tied to the wider Iran war.

Why it matters: Saudi Arabia is one of the world's largest oil exporters, and attacks near its oil sites can move prices everywhere. My read: even when damage is small, missiles over Riyadh show the Gulf war has more than one front, which would make any US-Iran deal harder to make stick.
topics.differences: The Houthis claim strikes on an airport and several oil facilities; Saudi Arabia says its defences intercepted the missiles and reports only minor damage from debris.[^18][^19] The death toll near Sanaa comes from the Houthi-run health ministry and has not been independently confirmed.[^18]

topics.heading: COP31 opens in Antalya with a fight over climate money and a warning on extremes
topics.summary: The UN climate summit opened in Turkey about 90 minutes late after overnight arguments over putting climate finance on the official agenda.[^20] UN chief António Guterres said the world has entered "a new age of climate extremes", as the WMO says 2026 is among the four hottest years on record.[^21]

lead.title: COP31 opens with early fight over climate finance

alsoReported.title: World enters 'new age of climate extremes', UN chief tells COP31
Ankara's COP31 message: electrify, recycle, don't mention coal

article: COP31, this year's UN climate summit, runs in Antalya, Turkey, from Nov 9 to 20, with Turkey as host and Australia leading the formal negotiations, an unusual shared arrangement.[^20] The opening started about 90 minutes late without explanation, after talks late on Sunday over developing countries' demand to put climate finance (money from richer countries to help poorer ones cut emissions and adapt) on the official agenda.[^20] A source told AFP a finance work programme will be included, but African countries did not win a separate item on tripling money for adaptation.[^20]

Guterres told delegates that "a supersized El Niño is colliding with a planet already superheated".[^21] The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says global temperatures from January to September were about 1.47°C above pre-industrial levels, and that this El Niño, a natural warming of the Pacific that heats the whole planet, is likely the strongest since at least 1950.[^21] One hopeful figure: countries with early warning systems for several hazards rose from 55 in 2015 to 136.[^21]

Turkey's main proposal is a voluntary "35 by 35" goal: electricity would supply 35% of the world's final energy use by 2035, up from about one-fifth today, according to the International Energy Agency.[^22] COP31's president, Murat Kurum, says electrification protects communities from volatile markets and cuts emissions.[^22] Critics, including Greenpeace Turkey, note the goal does not require the extra electricity to be clean, and Turkey still gets about a third of its own power from coal.[^22][^23]

The US government sent no officials, though a congressional delegation is attending, and the war around Hormuz hangs over the energy talks.[^20][^22] A senior EU official warned there is "no political will" for new funding pledges.[^20] My read: the real test is whether money for poorer countries moves at all; an electricity target is easier to agree than who pays.
topics.differences: Turkey says electrification is "the answer"; the EU wants the goal tied to clean power, and climate groups say that without it the goal could lock in coal and gas.[^20][^22][^23] Pacific island states want a clear roadmap away from fossil fuels, while Saudi Arabia and other producers say fossil fuels can stay if paired with carbon capture.[^22]

topics.heading: US voters back local limits on AI data centres, and tech stocks swing
topics.summary: In the Nov 3 elections, voters passed 39 local measures restricting AI data centres, and the Nasdaq fell sharply on Nov 5 before chip stocks recovered on Nov 6.[^26][^28] AI companies now face local worries about power, water and secret deals.[^24]

lead.title: After the midterms, things are looking rocky for Elon Musk and data centers

alsoReported.title: AI stocks plunge after US election, driving down markets
Americans overwhelmingly voted against data centers in the midterms

article: Data centres are huge buildings full of computer chips that train and run AI systems, and they use large amounts of electricity and, in some places, water. In last week's US elections, voters decided 45 local ballot measures about them, and 39 restrictive measures passed, according to Reuters as published by Al Jazeera; only North Dakota voted against restrictions.[^26] The measures included bans, pauses on new building, energy-use limits and requirements for public approval; restrictions won all 20 votes in Ohio, Engadget reports.[^27]

Investors reacted. On Nov 5 the tech-heavy Nasdaq index fell about 4.8% at midday, its steepest drop since April 2025, with chipmaker Nvidia down 8.2%.[^26] The bank UBS estimates construction pauses could put about 30% of planned new US data-centre capacity for 2028 at risk.[^26] The next day, chip stocks rebounded about 4%, helped by strong US jobs numbers.[^28]

TechCrunch reports that measures to speed up building were "nearly all defeated", and that local concerns include secret deals, officials signing non-disclosure agreements, and water use in the dry Southwest. OpenAI has responded with a blueprint for "compute campuses" without such agreements.[^24] Separately, the Justice Department launched a "Super Intelligence Task Force" to pursue foreign state actors, criminal groups and AI-enabled fraud.[^25]

How much this moved voters is debated. An NBC exit poll found 56% of voters called AI and data centres a crucial or major factor, but a TechCrunch editor argues it was not the main driver of the results, even if it is a grassroots issue in both parties.[^27][^24] My read: the AI boom depends on building in real towns, and local consent is becoming as real a limit as chips or money.
topics.differences: Analysts disagree on the sell-off: eToro saw a political risk premium "unwinding", while Swissquote saw investors moving away from US tech.[^28][^26] An exit poll suggests AI was a major issue for most voters; TechCrunch's Kirsten Korosec says it was not the main driver of the results.[^27][^24]
